analysis.one_liner: Caps payouts to people injured by defective products and gives manufacturers broad new defenses against lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill cleared a House committee on a 26-17 vote in March 1995 but never received a vote by the full House and died when the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the rules for lawsuits over defective products nationwide. It would cap compensation for pain and suffering at $250,000 or twice the financial loss, whichever is greater, limit punitive damages, and give manufacturers a complete defense if a federal agency approved the product or its label — including drugs and medical devices approved by the FDA. It would also bar lawsuits filed more than a set number of years after a product was first sold, and let defendants blame a worker's employer for the harm.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers and sellers of consumer products, drug and device makers, and their insurers gain the most: they would face caps on damages, new complete defenses, reduced joint liability, and shorter windows for lawsuits. Employers and workers' compensation insurers would gain a right to take a share of any settlement an injured worker receives.

how_it_helps.text: Caps compensation for pain and suffering at the greater of $250,000 or twice the actual financial loss, and limits punitive damages to the greater of $250,000 or three times the economic injury [S4].

Gives a manufacturer a complete defense if the product met a federal standard or labeling requirement, and bars suits over FDA-approved drugs and devices unless the maker withheld or misrepresented key safety information [S4].
Replaces joint liability with several liability for non-economic damages, so each defendant pays only its own percentage of responsibility [S4].
Imposes a two-year limit for filing suit and, for workplace injuries involving capital goods, a 15-year cutoff measured from the product's first sale [S4].

Makes a claimant's intoxication a complete defense where the claimant was more than 50 percent responsible for the event, and gives employers and workers' comp insurers subrogation rights over injured workers' recoveries [S4].

analysis.who_pays: People injured by defective products bear the cost. Someone permanently disabled by a faulty product with no lost wages would be limited to $250,000 for a lifetime of pain and suffering; victims of approved drugs with undisclosed problems could lose their day in court; and families suing over long-latency harm could run out of time.

drawbacks.text: A hard cap on non-economic damages pays a paralyzed or disfigured victim the same as a minor injury, as long as neither had large financial losses [S4].

The complete defense for FDA-approved drugs and devices shifts the cost of injuries from manufacturers to victims, even where a safer design was possible, unless the maker fraudulently withheld information from the FDA [S4].
Requiring 85 percent of punitive damages to go to the Treasury rather than the plaintiff weakens the financial incentive for victims to bring cases that punish willful misconduct [S4].

Letting manufacturers argue that a worker's employer or co-worker caused the harm puts injured employees in the position of helping prove their own boss's fault, with the employer joining the case against them [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Businesses would get more predictable liability exposure, which supporters argued would lower prices and reduce defensive design choices. But the costs fall entirely on a narrow, easily identified group — people already hurt by defective products — and the deepest cuts, such as the FDA-approval defense and the non-economic damages cap, apply precisely to the most seriously injured. The bill's protections for sellers whose manufacturers are unreachable, and its carve-outs for environmental claims, soften but do not change that balance.

outcome.mechanism: The House Commerce Committee approved it 26-17 and reported it in March 1995, but no bill ever came to the House floor, and the effort ended when the Congress expired in January 1997.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Oxley introduced the bill on February 13, 1995, and it was sent to both the Judiciary and Commerce Committees [S1].
A Commerce subcommittee held a hearing on February 21, 1995, and the full committee marked it up over two days, ordering it reported on a 26-17 roll-call vote [S6].

The committee reported an amended version on March 1, 1995 (H. Rept. 104-63, Part I), which tightened the punitive damages standard and added a 15-year cutoff and biomaterials supplier protections [S3, S6].
No further action appears in the record: the bill never reached the House floor, and it died at the end of the 104th Congress on January 3, 1997 [S1, S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured consumers keep the lawsuit rights the bill would have limited, while manufacturers, drug and device makers, and their insurers avoid the new defenses they sought. Separately, the broader product liability effort of that Congress (a different bill, H.R. 956) passed both chambers but was vetoed, so the industry remained subject to state tort law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Manufacturers keep facing state tort law; consumers keep lawsuit rights

sides.party_line_note: The record shows no floor vote and no cosponsors [S5]; the only recorded tally is the committee's 26-17 vote, whose party breakdown the provided sources do not give.

industries.note: The bill caps the damages they pay, gives them complete defenses based on federal standards and FDA approval, and shortens the window for lawsuits. Each gain comes directly out of what injured consumers could recover.

FDA premarket approval or general recognition as safe and effective would become a complete defense, even for injuries a safer design could have prevented, unless the company withheld information from the FDA.

They gain subrogation rights to intercept part of an injured worker's recovery and a voice in the worker's lawsuit, but they also lose the ability to seek indemnity from other wrongdoers and would be reimbursed for legal fees when the worker wins.

Damage caps, sanctions for frivolous pleadings, and a 15-year cutoff reduce the value and availability of product liability cases, which are often taken on contingency by attorneys representing individual victims.
